events.title: John Smyth baptises himself and his congregation in Amsterdam
events.summary: English Separatist exiles led by John Smyth and Thomas Helwys concluded that infant baptism was invalid and that a true church is a gathered fellowship of baptised believers. Smyth baptised himself (a 'se-baptism') and then the rest of the congregation, forming what is usually counted as the first English Baptist church. Helwys led part of the group back to London in 1612, founding the first Baptist congregation on English soil.
causes: Separatist conviction that the Church of England was not a true church
Reading of the New Testament as teaching baptism of confessing believers only
Contact with Waterlander Mennonites in Amsterdam
consequences: Origin of the General (Arminian) Baptists
Helwys's plea for religious liberty for all, including non-Christians (1612)
Smyth himself later sought union with the Mennonites, doubting his self-baptism

events.title: First London Confession of the Particular Baptists
events.summary: Seven Calvinistic ('Particular') Baptist congregations in London issued a joint confession to distinguish themselves from Anabaptists and to show their orthodoxy. Its 1646 revision added that baptism should be by immersion ('dipping'), which these congregations had adopted around 1641–42.
causes: Rise of Calvinistic Baptist congregations out of the Jacob–Lathrop–Jessey Independent church from the 1630s
Accusations linking all Baptists with the Münster rebellion
Civil War-era freedom to publish
consequences: Defined Particular Baptist identity alongside the Westminster Confession tradition
Prepared the way for the Second London Confession (1677/1689), still used by Reformed Baptists

events.title: Founding of the Southern Baptist Convention at Augusta
events.summary: In May 1845 Baptists from the slaveholding states met in Augusta, Georgia, and formed the Southern Baptist Convention after the national Baptist mission bodies refused to appoint slaveholders as missionaries. The split was over slavery: Southern delegates defended the right of slaveholders to serve, and the new convention's founders included many enslavers. The SBC formally repudiated this history in a 1995 resolution on racial reconciliation, apologising to African Americans and acknowledging that the convention had been founded in part to defend slavery.
causes: The Home Mission Society declined in 1844 to appoint the Georgia slaveholder James E. Reeve as a missionary (a deliberate test case)
The Boston-based foreign mission board's reply to the 'Alabama Resolutions' that it would not appoint a slaveholder
Sectional tensions that also split the Methodists (1844) and Presbyterians
consequences: Creation of what became the largest Protestant denomination in the United States
Northern Baptists continued in the older societies, organising as the Northern Baptist Convention in 1907
Freed Black Baptists formed their own conventions after emancipation
1995 SBC resolution repenting of the convention's defence of slavery and racism

events.title: Formation of the National Baptist Convention in Atlanta
events.summary: In September 1895 three African American Baptist bodies — the Foreign Mission Baptist Convention (1880), the American National Baptist Convention (1886) and the Baptist National Educational Convention (1893) — merged in Atlanta to form the National Baptist Convention of the United States of America, the largest Black denomination in the country.
causes: Explosive growth of independent Black Baptist churches after emancipation
Desire for Black-led missions to Africa, publishing and education
Exclusion and paternalism in white-led Baptist bodies
consequences: 1915 split over control of the publishing board produced the National Baptist Convention of America
1961 split over leadership and civil-rights strategy produced the Progressive National Baptist Convention, the denominational home of Martin Luther King Jr.
Black Baptist churches became central institutions of the civil rights movement

events.title: First Brethren baptisms in the Eder at Schwarzenau
events.summary: Eight Radical Pietists led by Alexander Mack, sheltering in the tolerant county of Sayn-Wittgenstein, baptised one another by threefold forward immersion in the river Eder in 1708. They intended to restore the New Testament church; their opponents called them Dunkers (from tunken, 'to dip').
causes: Radical Pietist rejection of state churches
Reading of Anabaptist and Pietist writers, including Gottfried Arnold
Persecution of separatists in the Palatinate
consequences: Origin of the Schwarzenau Brethren (Church of the Brethren and related bodies)
Migration to Pennsylvania from 1719, with the Germantown congregation formed in 1723
Later branches: Old German Baptist Brethren (1881), Brethren Church (1883), Grace Brethren

events.title: The Bethesda controversy divides the Brethren
events.summary: When Bethesda Chapel in Bristol, led by George Müller and Henry Craik, received worshippers from B. W. Newton's Plymouth assembly — whose Christological teaching John Nelson Darby had condemned — Darby issued a circular in August 1848 calling for assemblies to refuse fellowship with Bethesda. The Brethren divided into 'Exclusive' assemblies, which held that a decision binds all connected meetings, and 'Open' assemblies, which treat each local assembly as autonomous.
causes: Dispute over B. W. Newton's teaching on Christ's sufferings
Competing views of church discipline and the unity of assemblies
Personal tensions between leading Brethren teachers
consequences: Permanent separation of Open and Exclusive Brethren
Further Exclusive divisions (1881, 1890 Raven, and later the Taylor-led Plymouth Brethren Christian Church)
Open Brethren became a major missionary movement in Africa, India and Latin America

events.title: Abolitionist Methodists form the Wesleyan Methodist Connection
events.summary: Abolitionist ministers including Orange Scott and Luther Lee left the Methodist Episcopal Church, which tolerated slaveholding members and clergy, and organised the Wesleyan Methodist Connection at Utica in May 1843. They forbade slaveholding, rejected episcopacy and gave laity a larger role.
causes: Methodist Episcopal Church compromise over slavery and suppression of abolitionist agitation
Revivalist and holiness concern for a pure church
consequences: Pressure contributed to the 1844 North–South division of the Methodist Episcopal Church
The Wesleyan Chapel at Seneca Falls hosted the 1848 Women's Rights Convention
Merged with the Pilgrim Holiness Church in 1968 to form the Wesleyan Church

events.title: Founding of the Free Methodist Church at Pekin
events.summary: After B. T. Roberts and other 'Nazarite' preachers were expelled from the Genesee Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church for criticising its worldliness, laity and ministers met at Pekin, New York, in August 1860 and organised the Free Methodist Church.
causes: Expulsion of Roberts (1858) for his critique of declining Methodist discipline
Opposition to rented pews, slaveholding and secret societies
Commitment to entire sanctification
consequences: 'Free' seats for the poor, freedom from slavery, and freedom in worship became the church's watchwords
Early advocacy (Roberts's Ordaining Women, 1891) for women in ministry

events.title: Holiness union at Pilot Point forms the Church of the Nazarene
events.summary: In October 1908 the Pentecostal Church of the Nazarene — itself the 1907 union of Phineas Bresee's Los Angeles Church of the Nazarene (1895) and the eastern Association of Pentecostal Churches of America — joined with the southern Holiness Church of Christ at Pilot Point, Texas. Nazarenes count this as their founding; 'Pentecostal' was dropped from the name in 1919 to avoid confusion with the tongues movement.
causes: Holiness believers leaving or expelled from Methodism over entire sanctification
Desire to unite regional holiness bodies into a national church
consequences: Largest denomination of the Wesleyan-Holiness tradition
Distinguished itself from Pentecostalism by rejecting tongues as the evidence of Spirit baptism

events.title: The 'New Issue': baptism in Jesus' name at the Arroyo Seco camp meeting
events.summary: At the Worldwide Apostolic Faith camp meeting at Arroyo Seco near Los Angeles in April 1913, R. E. McAlister remarked that the apostles baptised in the name of Jesus only. Frank Ewart and Glenn Cook began rebaptising believers in Jesus' name in 1914, teaching that Jesus is the name of the one God. In 1916 the Assemblies of God adopted a Trinitarian Statement of Fundamental Truths and about a quarter of its ministers left.
causes: Restorationist reading of Acts 2:38 and the 'finished work' teaching of William Durham
Pentecostal expectation of fresh revelation
consequences: Origin of Oneness (Apostolic) Pentecostalism, outside historic Nicene Trinitarianism
Formation of the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World and later the United Pentecostal Church International

events.title: Swedish missionaries found the Assembleia de Deus in Belém
events.summary: Daniel Berg and Gunnar Vingren, Swedish Baptists who had received Spirit baptism in Chicago, arrived in Belém in 1910. Expelled from the local Baptist church with eighteen followers in June 1911, they formed the Apostolic Faith Mission, renamed the Assembleia de Deus in 1918.
causes: Influence of William Durham's Chicago revival
Prophecy directing Berg and Vingren to Pará
Rubber-boom migration in the Amazon
consequences: Grew into Brazil's largest Protestant family and one of the largest Pentecostal movements in the world
Fragmented into many conventions and ministries (CGADB, CONAMAD and others)

events.title: Bible Students divide after the death of Charles Taze Russell
events.summary: After Russell died in October 1916, Joseph F. Rutherford became president of the Watch Tower Society in January 1917. His removal of four directors and the publication of The Finished Mystery that year divided the Bible Students. Many who remained loyal to Russell's writings formed independent fellowships such as the Pastoral Bible Institute (1918) and the Dawn Bible Students; those who stayed with the Society took the name Jehovah's witnesses in 1931.
causes: Disputed succession and Rutherford's centralisation of authority
Disagreement over whether Russell's Studies in the Scriptures were final
consequences: Separate history of Independent Bible Students
Rutherford-era doctrinal and organisational changes in what became Jehovah's Witnesses

events.title: Joseph Smith III accepts leadership of the Reorganized Church at Amboy
events.summary: On 6 April 1860 at Amboy, Illinois, Joseph Smith III, son of the Latter Day Saint founder, accepted the presidency of the 'New Organization' of Saints who had rejected Brigham Young's leadership and plural marriage. The body became the Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, renamed Community of Christ in 2001.
causes: Succession crisis after Joseph Smith's death in 1844
Rejection of Brigham Young's leadership and of polygamy
Belief in lineal succession of the prophetic office
consequences: Largest Latter Day Saint body after the Utah church
Later moved toward mainstream Protestant theology, ordaining women from 1984

events.title: U.S. Religious Census lists the Churches of Christ separately
events.summary: At the request of David Lipscomb, editor of the Gospel Advocate, the 1906 U.S. Census of Religious Bodies listed the 'Churches of Christ' separately from the 'Disciples of Christ', formally recognising a division in the Stone-Campbell movement that had been widening for decades, largely along Northern/Southern and urban/rural lines.
causes: Dispute over instrumental music in worship and missionary societies
Different readings of the silence of Scripture (what the New Testament does not authorise)
Post–Civil War sectional and economic divides
consequences: Churches of Christ (a cappella) as a distinct fellowship
Disciples and the later independent Christian Churches developed separately

events.title: The Worldwide Church of God embraces Nicene Christianity
events.summary: After Herbert W. Armstrong's death (1986), the leadership of the Worldwide Church of God under Joseph W. Tkach re-examined Armstrong's teachings. The church adopted the doctrine of the Trinity (1993) and, in a December 1994 sermon, Tkach announced that Christians are not bound by Old Covenant laws such as the Saturday Sabbath, festivals and dietary rules. It is a rare case of a whole denomination moving into historic orthodoxy.
causes: Study of Armstrong's teachings by the post-1986 leadership
Engagement with evangelical scholars
consequences: Large splinter groups formed to keep Armstrong's teachings (United Church of God, 1995; Living Church of God, 1998)
Membership and income fell sharply
Admitted to the National Association of Evangelicals (1997); renamed Grace Communion International (2009)

events.title: Inauguration of the Church of North India at Nagpur
events.summary: On 29 November 1970 six churches — the United Church of Northern India (Presbyterian and Congregational), the Anglican Church of India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon (northern dioceses), the Council of Baptist Churches in Northern India, the Methodist Church (British and Australian conferences), the Church of the Brethren in India and the Disciples of Christ — united as the Church of North India.
causes: Example of the Church of South India (1947)
Missionary and Indian desire to end imported Western divisions
Decades of negotiation (Plan of Union 1951–65)
consequences: First union to include Baptists and to reconcile believers' and infant baptism within one church
Full communion with the Anglican Communion and member of the World Methodist Council and WCRC
The Church of Pakistan formed the same year

events.title: Inauguration of the United Church of Canada
events.summary: On 10 June 1925 at the Mutual Street Arena in Toronto, the Methodist Church (Canada), the Congregational Union of Canada, about two-thirds of the Presbyterian Church in Canada and the local union churches of the West united as the United Church of Canada. A third of Presbyterians, voting against union, continued the Presbyterian Church in Canada.
causes: Prairie settlements unable to support competing denominations
Social Gospel and nation-building ideals
Two decades of negotiation (Basis of Union, 1908)
consequences: Became Canada's largest Protestant church
Lasting legal and pastoral bitterness with continuing Presbyterians
Later formal apologies for its role in residential schools (1986, 1998)

events.title: Formation of the Uniting Church in Australia
events.summary: On 22 June 1977 the Methodist Church of Australasia, most of the Presbyterian Church of Australia and most of the Congregational Union of Australia joined to form the Uniting Church in Australia, on the Basis of Union agreed in 1971. About a third of Presbyterian congregations continued as the Presbyterian Church of Australia.
causes: Ecumenical movement and shared mission in the outback (e.g. the Australian Inland Mission)
Negotiations since 1957
consequences: Uniting Aboriginal and Islander Christian Congress (1985) and covenant with it (1994)
2009 constitutional Preamble acknowledging First Peoples' prior presence

events.title: Uniting General Synod forms the United Church of Christ
events.summary: On 25 June 1957 in Cleveland, the Evangelical and Reformed Church (a 1934 union of German Reformed and Evangelical Synod churches) and the General Council of the Congregational Christian Churches united as the United Church of Christ. A Statement of Faith followed in 1959.
causes: Ecumenical hopes for American Protestant unity
Mainline cooperation after the Second World War
consequences: Some Congregational churches stayed out, forming the National Association of Congregational Christian Churches (1955) and the Conservative Congregational Christian Conference
Joined the Formula of Agreement (1997) with Lutherans, Presbyterians and Reformed

events.title: Formation of the United Church of Christ in Japan (Kyodan)
events.summary: In June 1941, under the Religious Organizations Law of 1939, some thirty Protestant denominations in Japan were brought into a single body, the Nihon Kirisuto Kyodan. Union was long desired by some Japanese Christians but was carried out under heavy state pressure in wartime.
causes: Religious Organizations Law (1939) requiring registration of large bodies
Wartime nationalism and suspicion of foreign-linked churches
Earlier Japanese ecumenical aspirations
consequences: After 1945 Anglicans, Lutherans, some Baptists, Holiness and Reformed groups withdrew
1967 'Confession on the Responsibility of the Kyodan During World War II' acknowledging complicity in the war

events.title: Felix Manalo registers the Iglesia ni Cristo
events.summary: On 27 July 1914 Felix Y. Manalo, who had passed through Methodist, Presbyterian, Christian Mission (Disciples) and Seventh-day Adventist churches, registered the Iglesia ni Cristo with the American colonial government. Its members regard Manalo as God's last messenger, the 'angel from the east' of Revelation 7:2, re-establishing the true church in the Philippines.
causes: Manalo's study of Scripture and conclusion that the church had apostatised
Nationalist sentiment under American colonial rule
consequences: Became one of the largest indigenous churches in Asia, with bloc-voting influence in Philippine politics
Leadership passed to Eraño Manalo (1963) and Eduardo Manalo (2009)

events.title: Union forms the United Methodist Church
events.summary: On 23 April 1968 in Dallas the Methodist Church and the Evangelical United Brethren Church united as the United Methodist Church. The same General Conference abolished the segregated Central Jurisdiction (created in 1939) that had grouped Black Methodist conferences separately.
causes: Shared Wesleyan and German Pietist heritage of the two churches
Mid-century ecumenism
Pressure of the civil rights movement against the Central Jurisdiction
consequences: Largest mainline Protestant church in the U.S. for decades
1972 language declaring homosexual practice incompatible with Christian teaching began a fifty-year dispute
2019–2023 disaffiliations and 2024 removal of restrictions

traditions.name: General Baptists
traditions.summary: The earliest English Baptists, descended from the congregation of John Smyth and Thomas Helwys (Amsterdam 1609, London 1612). They were called 'General' because they held that Christ died for all people generally (an Arminian view of the atonement). Many older General Baptist congregations drifted toward Unitarianism in the eighteenth century; the evangelical New Connexion (1770) merged with the Particular Baptists in 1891, and American heirs include the Free Will Baptists and the General Association of General Baptists.
distinctives: Early advocacy of liberty of conscience (Helwys, 1612)
Messengers linking congregations into an Assembly
Some practised laying on of hands after baptism (Hebrews 6:1-2)

profile.authority: Scripture alone, interpreted within the gathered congregation; confessions such as the Standard Confession (1660) as summaries, not binding creeds.
profile.salvation: Christ died for all; grace enables a free response of faith, and believers can fall away.
profile.sacraments: Two ordinances, baptism of professing believers and the Lord's Supper; originally baptism by pouring, later immersion.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return, resurrection and final judgment.
profile.governance: Congregational, with messengers and a General Assembly linking churches.
profile.worship: Plain preaching services; some early congregations resisted congregational hymn singing.

traditions.status: Historic as a separate English movement; continues in small General Baptist bodies and in the Free Will Baptist tradition.

traditions.name: Particular (Calvinistic) Baptists
traditions.summary: Calvinistic Baptists who emerged from London Independent (Congregationalist) churches in the 1630s. They held that Christ died for a 'particular' people, the elect. Their First (1644) and Second (1677, published 1689) London Confessions closely follow Reformed theology; leaders included William Kiffin, Hanserd Knollys, Benjamin Keach and later John Gill and Andrew Fuller, whose evangelical Calvinism inspired the Baptist Missionary Society (1792).
distinctives: Calvinist soteriology with believers' baptism by immersion
Covenant theology in a Baptist key
Fuller's 'evangelical Calvinism' launched modern Protestant missions

profile.authority: Scripture alone; the Second London Confession (1689) as a widely used standard among Reformed Baptists.
profile.salvation: Unconditional election, particular redemption, effectual grace and perseverance of the saints.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion of professing believers and the Lord's Supper as ordinances, often with a spiritual-presence view.
profile.eschatology: Generally amillennial or postmillennial in the classical period; premillennialism later spread among some.
profile.governance: Congregational, with associations for fellowship and mission.
profile.worship: Preaching-centred services; Benjamin Keach championed congregational hymn singing.

traditions.status: Historic name; the tradition continues in Reformed Baptist churches and as a strand within most Baptist bodies.

traditions.name: Southern Baptist Convention
traditions.summary: Founded at Augusta, Georgia, in 1845 when Baptists of the slave states separated from the national Baptist mission societies over the appointment of slaveholders as missionaries. The SBC grew into the largest Protestant denomination in the United States, with a powerful cooperative mission programme (Cooperative Program, 1925; International Mission Board). A 'conservative resurgence' from 1979 shifted its seminaries and agencies toward biblical inerrancy. In 1995 it formally apologised for its origins in the defence of slavery and for its support of segregation.
distinctives: Cooperative Program funding of missions and seminaries
Strong emphasis on evangelism and church planting
Complementarian limits on women as pastors (2000; affirmed 2023)
Autonomy of local churches within voluntary convention structures

profile.authority: Scripture as inspired and without error; the Baptist Faith and Message (1925, 1963, 2000) as a consensus statement, not a creed binding churches.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through personal faith in Christ; once saved, always saved (perseverance) is widely held; Calvinist and non-Calvinist streams coexist.
profile.sacraments: Two ordinances: believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as a memorial.
profile.eschatology: Return of Christ, judgment, heaven and hell; premillennialism common but no single view required.
profile.governance: Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions. The annual convention elects officers and trustees of agencies.
profile.worship: Revivalist-style services with preaching, congregational song and an invitation to respond.

traditions.status: Active; c. 12.7 million members in c. 47,000 churches (2024), with membership declining since 2006.

traditions.name: National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc.
traditions.summary: The largest African American denomination, formed in Atlanta in 1895 from three Black Baptist conventions. It sustained missions in Africa and the Caribbean, publishing and schools. Its 1915 split produced the National Baptist Convention of America, and in 1961 supporters of a more activist civil-rights strategy, including Martin Luther King Jr., formed the Progressive National Baptist Convention.
distinctives: Black-led Baptist institutions independent of white control
Preaching tradition central to Black church life
Missions to Liberia and southern Africa
Churches as centres of community and civil-rights organising

profile.authority: Scripture alone, commonly summarised in the New Hampshire Confession (1833) tradition.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ, received in conversion.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper as ordinances.
profile.eschatology: Hope of Christ's return and final deliverance, often linked with themes of exodus and freedom.
profile.governance: Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions.
profile.worship: Expressive worship with gospel music, call-and-response preaching and devotion services.

traditions.status: Active; one of the largest Black denominations in the United States (membership self-reported in the millions).

traditions.name: American Baptist Churches USA
traditions.summary: Heirs of the northern Baptist mission societies (Triennial Convention 1814; Home Mission Society 1832) that remained after the 1845 Southern split. Organised as the Northern Baptist Convention (1907), renamed the American Baptist Convention (1950) and American Baptist Churches USA (1972). A theologically diverse, ecumenical body, it was the church of Walter Rauschenbusch and a founding member of the Federal, National and World Councils of Churches; it ordains women.
distinctives: Historic home of the Social Gospel
Wide theological range from evangelical to liberal

profile.authority: Scripture as the authoritative witness to Christ, interpreted in freedom of conscience; no binding confession.
profile.salvation: Salvation through faith in Jesus Christ; emphasis on personal and social transformation.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Varied; classical hope of Christ's return and the kingdom of God.
profile.governance: Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions. Regional associations and national boards.
profile.worship: Free-church services with hymns, preaching and lay participation.

traditions.status: Active; roughly 1.1 million members reported in recent years, with several regions having left over sexuality debates.

traditions.name: Seventh Day Baptists
traditions.summary: Baptists who keep the seventh day (Saturday) as the Sabbath. Sabbatarian Baptist congregations appeared in England in the 1650s (Mill Yard, London); the first American church was organised at Newport, Rhode Island, in 1671. Seventh Day Baptist teaching on the Sabbath influenced the early Adventists in the 1840s.
distinctives: Early Sabbatarian witness in England and New England
Link to the Adventist adoption of the Sabbath (Rachel Oakes Preston, 1844)

profile.authority: Scripture alone; the Bible's commandment of the seventh-day Sabbath taken as still binding.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith; Sabbath-keeping as grateful obedience, not a means of salvation.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return and judgment.
profile.governance: Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions. A General Conference (1802) and a World Federation link churches.
profile.worship: Saturday worship with preaching and hymns.

traditions.status: Active but small; congregations in North America, Africa, Asia and Latin America linked by the Seventh Day Baptist World Federation.

traditions.name: Free Will Baptists
traditions.summary: Arminian Baptists in the General Baptist line. Paul Palmer organised a church in Chowan County, North Carolina, in 1727, and Benjamin Randall founded a northern Free Will Baptist movement at New Durham, New Hampshire, in 1780. The northern body merged with the Northern Baptists in 1911; southern churches formed the National Association of Free Will Baptists in 1935.
distinctives: Feet washing as an ordinance in many churches

profile.authority: Scripture alone; the Treatise of the Faith and Practices of Free Will Baptists.
profile.salvation: Christ died for all; salvation is conditioned on faith, and a believer may forfeit salvation by unbelief.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and, in many churches, washing of the saints' feet.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return, judgment and eternal destinies.
profile.governance: Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions.
profile.worship: Revivalist and gospel-song services; communion often followed by feet washing.

traditions.status: Active; National Association of Free Will Baptists and related bodies.

traditions.name: Nigerian Baptist Convention
traditions.summary: Grew from the Southern Baptist mission of Thomas Jefferson Bowen, who reached Yorubaland in 1850, and from Yoruba Baptist leaders who carried the work forward when American missionaries withdrew during the U.S. Civil War. The Yoruba Baptist Association (1914) became the Nigerian Baptist Convention, one of the largest Baptist bodies outside the United States. African Baptist churches also arose from the 1888 'Native Baptist' secession over missionary control.
distinctives: Evangelism across Nigeria and West Africa

profile.authority: Scripture alone; Baptist confessional statements adapted from Southern Baptist models.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return.
profile.governance: Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions. Conferences and an elected president and general secretary.
profile.worship: Yoruba and English services with choirs, indigenous music and preaching.

traditions.status: Active; one of the largest member bodies of the Baptist World Alliance, with membership reported in the millions.

traditions.name: Brazilian Baptist Convention (Convenção Batista Brasileira)
traditions.summary: Formed in 1907 from churches planted after Southern Baptist missionaries William and Anne Bagby and Zachary and Kate Taylor organised the first Portuguese-speaking Baptist church in Salvador, Bahia, in 1882. Brazilian Baptists became one of the largest Baptist communities in the world and sent missionaries abroad; a charismatic wing separated in 1965 as the National Baptist Convention (CBN).
distinctives: Strong home and foreign mission boards

profile.authority: Scripture alone; Brazilian Baptist Declaration of Faith.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return.
profile.governance: Congregational: each local church is autonomous under Christ, calling its own pastor and deacons; churches cooperate voluntarily through associations and conventions.
profile.worship: Evangelistic services with congregational singing and preaching.

traditions.status: Active; a major member body of the Baptist World Alliance.

traditions.name: Plymouth Brethren
traditions.summary: A movement of believers who began meeting simply to 'break bread' outside the established churches in Dublin in the late 1820s; the large assembly at Plymouth (from 1831) gave the movement its popular name. Leaders included Anthony Norris Groves, B. W. Newton, George Müller and John Nelson Darby, whose dispensationalism and pre-tribulation rapture teaching spread far beyond the Brethren. They divided in 1848 into Open and Exclusive branches.
distinctives: No ordained clergy; open participation of brothers in worship
Gathering in the name of the Lord alone, without denominational labels

profile.authority: Scripture alone, studied by all believers; no creeds.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith, with strong assurance.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism (mostly immersion) and the weekly Lord's Supper as remembrance.
profile.eschatology: Dispensational premillennialism, with a pre-tribulation rapture.
profile.governance: Local assemblies led by a plurality of elders; no clergy-laity distinction.
profile.worship: Unstructured worship meeting around the Lord's Table, with participation by men; women usually silent and head-covered.

traditions.status: Active in Open and Exclusive branches worldwide.

traditions.name: Open Brethren
traditions.summary: The branch of the Brethren that, after the 1848 Bethesda controversy, treated each assembly as independent in receiving members and exercising discipline. Open Brethren became a major source of 'faith' missionaries, including Anthony Norris Groves in India and F. S. Arnot in central Africa (Echoes of Service), and are numerous in India, Zambia, Angola and Latin America.
distinctives: Open reception of believers to the Lord's Table
Faith missions (Echoes of Service, Christian Missions in Many Lands)

profile.authority: Scripture alone.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by immersion and weekly breaking of bread.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial, mostly dispensational.
profile.governance: Autonomous assemblies led by elders; some now employ full-time workers.
profile.worship: Breaking of bread meeting with open participation, plus preaching services.

traditions.status: Active; especially strong in India, Zambia, Angola, Latin America and the English-speaking world.

traditions.name: Exclusive Brethren
traditions.summary: The branch of the Brethren following John Nelson Darby after 1848, holding that assemblies form one connected fellowship whose disciplinary decisions bind all. Further divisions followed; the largest present body, the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church (formerly the Taylor–Symington–Hales line), practises strict separation from non-members, which critics and former members describe as harmful to family relationships and which the church defends as biblical holiness.
distinctives: Interconnected assemblies bound by common discipline
Separation from evil as a principle of unity
Some branches practise strict social separation

profile.authority: Scripture alone, with Darby's writings and those of later leading teachers highly valued.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (in some branches including household baptism of children) and weekly Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Dispensational premillennialism with pre-tribulation rapture.
profile.governance: Fellowship of assemblies; in some branches a recognised universal leader.
profile.worship: Lord's Supper and ministry meetings; men speak, women head-covered.

traditions.status: Active in several separate fellowships; the PBCC is the largest.

traditions.name: Church of the Brethren (Schwarzenau Brethren)
traditions.summary: Founded in 1708 when Alexander Mack and seven others baptised one another in the river Eder at Schwarzenau, combining Radical Pietism with Anabaptist convictions. Persecuted in Europe, the Brethren ('Dunkers') moved to Pennsylvania from 1719. One of the three historic peace churches, with a large church in Nigeria (Ekklesiyar Yan'uwa a Nigeria, EYN) that has suffered heavily from Boko Haram attacks.
distinctives: Love feast with feet washing, fellowship meal and communion
No force in religion; no creed but the New Testament
Simple living and service (Brethren Volunteer Service, Heifer Project origins)

profile.authority: The New Testament as the rule of faith and practice, read in community; no formal creed.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace received in faith and lived in obedient discipleship.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by trine immersion; the love feast, combining feet washing, a fellowship meal and the bread and cup; anointing of the sick.
profile.eschatology: Hope of Christ's return; little speculative emphasis.
profile.governance: Congregational with an Annual Conference as the highest authority.
profile.worship: Simple services; love feast observed periodically.

traditions.status: Active; the U.S. church has declined, while EYN in Nigeria is larger.

traditions.name: Brethren in Christ Church
traditions.summary: Arose about 1778 among Mennonite and Pietist believers in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania (the 'River Brethren', after the Susquehanna), who sought a personal conversion experience alongside Anabaptist discipleship. From the 1910s it absorbed Wesleyan holiness teaching. Its largest membership today is in Zimbabwe, Zambia and other African and Asian countries.
distinctives: Blend of Anabaptist, Pietist and Wesleyan holiness streams
Strong missions in southern Africa and India

profile.authority: Scripture as final authority, interpreted in community.
profile.salvation: New birth by grace through faith, followed by sanctification and discipleship.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by trine immersion, the Lord's Supper and feet washing.
profile.eschatology: Hope of Christ's return.
profile.governance: Conference-based with bishops/overseers.
profile.worship: Evangelical worship with Anabaptist simplicity.

traditions.status: Active; member of Mennonite World Conference.

traditions.name: Evangelical Free Church
traditions.summary: Free churches formed by Scandinavian Pietists who left or were pushed out of Lutheran state churches. In the United States the Swedish Evangelical Free Church (1884) and Norwegian-Danish free church associations merged in 1950 to form the Evangelical Free Church of America (EFCA), known for a short Statement of Faith and for majoring on essentials. Trinity Evangelical Divinity School is its seminary.
distinctives: Congregational free church from Scandinavian Pietism

profile.authority: Scripture as inerrant Word of God; EFCA Statement of Faith.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ alone.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper as ordinances; both believer's and infant baptism historically tolerated.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial return of Christ.
profile.governance: Congregational, with a cooperative national association.
profile.worship: Contemporary evangelical worship.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Evangelical Covenant Church
traditions.summary: Founded in Chicago in 1885 by Swedish immigrant Mission Friends, heirs of the Swedish Pietist revival (Carl Olof Rosenius, Paul Peter Waldenström) that formed the Mission Covenant Church of Sweden (1878). The Covenant asks 'Where is it written?' and seeks freedom in non-essentials, permitting both infant and believer's baptism.
distinctives: Pietist heritage of conversion and devotional life
'Where is it written?' — biblical question as test
Both infant and believer baptism practised

profile.authority: Scripture as the only perfect rule for faith, doctrine and conduct.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith; new life in Christ.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (infants or believers) and the Lord's Supper as sacraments.
profile.eschatology: Hope of Christ's return without a fixed millennial view.
profile.governance: Congregational with a connectional covenant of churches.
profile.worship: Evangelical worship with Scandinavian hymn heritage.

traditions.status: Active; in 2023 it expelled a regional conference and churches over affirmation of same-sex relationships.

traditions.name: Christian and Missionary Alliance
traditions.summary: Founded in 1887 by the former Presbyterian minister A. B. Simpson in New York as two societies (Christian Alliance and Evangelical Missionary Alliance) merged in 1897. Simpson's 'Fourfold Gospel' (Christ as Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer and Coming King) shaped early Pentecostalism, though the Alliance rejected tongues as the necessary evidence of the Spirit. Its missions produced large churches in Vietnam, Indonesia, Gabon and elsewhere.
distinctives: Became a denomination only gradually (1974 in USA)

profile.authority: Scripture as inerrant Word of God.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith; a subsequent crisis of sanctification and ongoing Spirit-filled life.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper; anointing of the sick for healing.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial return of Christ as a motive for missions.
profile.governance: Mixed: local churches with a General Council and districts.
profile.worship: Evangelical worship.

traditions.status: Active; international Alliance World Fellowship.

traditions.name: Moravian Church (Renewed Unitas Fratrum)
traditions.summary: The renewal of the old Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum) among refugees from Moravia on Count Nicolaus von Zinzendorf's estate at Herrnhut, Saxony, where a profound communion service on 13 August 1727 is remembered as its spiritual birthday. From 1732 Moravians pioneered Protestant world mission (Caribbean, Greenland, Suriname, South Africa) and deeply influenced John Wesley. The largest provinces today are in Tanzania.
distinctives: Heart religion centred on the wounds and love of Christ
Episcopacy maintained from the old Unity

profile.authority: Scripture as the sole standard of doctrine; ecumenical creeds and the Augsburg Confession respected; Ground of the Unity (1957).
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in the crucified Christ; personal relationship with the Saviour.
profile.sacraments: Infant and believer baptism and Holy Communion; the love feast as a fellowship meal.
profile.eschatology: Hope in Christ's return; emphasis on the present reign of Christ.
profile.governance: Unity of autonomous provinces with synods; bishops have a pastoral and ordaining role.
profile.worship: Liturgical singing, love feasts, Easter sunrise services in God's Acre.

traditions.status: Active; c. one million members worldwide, a majority in Africa.

traditions.name: African Methodist Episcopal Church
traditions.summary: The first independent Black denomination in the United States, organised in Philadelphia in 1816 under Richard Allen after Black Methodists withdrew from St George's Methodist Episcopal Church in protest at segregation. The AME Church spread across the South after emancipation, founded Wilberforce University (1856) and established strong conferences in southern and western Africa.

profile.authority: Scripture, with the Methodist Articles of Religion and AME Discipline.
profile.salvation: Wesleyan: universal grace, justification by faith, assurance and holiness.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (including infants) and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Classical hope of Christ's return, with strong themes of liberation.
profile.governance: Episcopal: bishops, annual conferences and a General Conference.
profile.worship: Methodist liturgy blended with Black church preaching and music.

traditions.status: Active; churches in the U.S., Caribbean and Africa.

traditions.name: African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church
traditions.summary: Grew from Black Methodists who left John Street Methodist Church in New York in 1796 over discrimination, forming Zion Church and in 1821 an independent connection. Known as 'the Freedom Church', it counted Harriet Tubman, Sojourner Truth and Frederick Douglass among its members and ordained women as elders in the 1890s.
distinctives: Early ordination of women (Julia Foote, Mary Small)
Missions in Ghana, Nigeria and Liberia

profile.authority: Scripture, Articles of Religion and the AME Zion Discipline.
profile.salvation: Wesleyan: free grace, justification by faith and holiness.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Classical hope of Christ's return.
profile.governance: Episcopal with conferences.
profile.worship: Methodist order with Black church musical tradition.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: United Methodist Church
traditions.summary: Formed in Dallas in 1968 by the union of the Methodist Church (itself a 1939 reunion of northern and southern Methodism and the Methodist Protestant Church) and the Evangelical United Brethren. Long the second-largest U.S. Protestant body, it is a worldwide church with growing conferences in Africa and the Philippines. After decades of dispute over sexuality, roughly a quarter of U.S. congregations left in 2019–2023, many joining the Global Methodist Church (2022); the 2024 General Conference removed restrictions on gay clergy and same-sex weddings.
distinctives: Connexional polity with bishops and itinerant appointment of clergy
Social Principles and Book of Resolutions
Ordination of women (full clergy rights since 1956)

profile.authority: Scripture as primary, interpreted with tradition, experience and reason; Articles of Religion, EUB Confession and Wesley's Sermons and Notes as doctrinal standards.
profile.salvation: Wesleyan: prevenient, justifying and sanctifying grace; salvation open to all.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (infants and adults) and Holy Communion as sacraments; open table.
profile.eschatology: Classical hope of resurrection and new creation.
profile.governance: Episcopal and connexional: General, jurisdictional, central and annual conferences; bishops appoint pastors.
profile.worship: Liturgical and free forms; Wesley hymns; the United Methodist Hymnal.

traditions.status: Active; reshaped by the 2019–2024 disaffiliations and regionalisation.

traditions.name: Free Methodist Church
traditions.summary: Organised at Pekin, New York, in 1860 after B. T. Roberts and others were expelled from the Methodist Episcopal Church for preaching a stricter holiness. It stood for free pews for the poor, opposition to slavery and secret societies, and entire sanctification. Now a worldwide holiness denomination.
distinctives: Early support for women in ministry

profile.authority: Scripture with the Free Methodist Articles of Religion.
profile.salvation: Wesleyan-Arminian with entire sanctification as a second work of grace.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Return of Christ and final judgment.
profile.governance: Conference with bishops.
profile.worship: Evangelical holiness worship.

traditions.status: Active; worldwide membership mostly outside North America.

traditions.name: Wesleyan Church
traditions.summary: Formed in 1968 by the merger of the Wesleyan Methodist Church, founded in 1843 by abolitionists leaving the Methodist Episcopal Church, and the Pilgrim Holiness Church (1897). Its seminary and universities (Indiana Wesleyan, Houghton) make it a significant voice of Wesleyan-Holiness evangelicalism.
distinctives: Ordination of women since its origins

profile.authority: Scripture as inerrant, with the Wesleyan Articles of Religion.
profile.salvation: Wesleyan-Arminian with entire sanctification.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Return of Christ.
profile.governance: Conference-based with a General Conference and general superintendents.
profile.worship: Evangelical worship.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Church of the Nazarene
traditions.summary: The largest Wesleyan-Holiness denomination, formed by the union of regional holiness churches culminating at Pilot Point, Texas, in 1908. Founders included Phineas F. Bresee of Los Angeles. It teaches entire sanctification as a second definite work of grace and has a strong international presence, with a majority of members outside the United States.
distinctives: Women in ministry from the beginning
Rejection of tongues as initial evidence

profile.authority: Scripture as inerrantly revealing God's will in matters of salvation; Articles of Faith in the Manual.
profile.salvation: Wesleyan-Arminian: justification by faith, followed by entire sanctification cleansing the heart from original sin.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (infants or believers; any mode) and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial return not required; Christ's return, resurrection and judgment.
profile.governance: Mixed episcopal-congregational: districts, district superintendents and general superintendents; General Assembly.
profile.worship: Evangelical holiness worship.

traditions.status: Active; self-reports about 2.6 million members worldwide.

traditions.name: Church of God (Anderson, Indiana)
traditions.summary: A holiness reformation movement begun by Daniel S. Warner in 1881, rejecting denominational structures as man-made divisions and calling Christians 'out of Babylon' into the visible unity of the one church of God. Headquartered in Anderson, Indiana, it remains non-Pentecostal and treats membership as conversion rather than enrolment.

profile.authority: Scripture alone; no creed.
profile.salvation: Wesleyan holiness: new birth and sanctification.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and feet washing.
profile.eschatology: Amillennial, historically reading Revelation as church history.
profile.governance: Congregational with cooperative ministries.
profile.worship: Evangelical holiness worship.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Korean Methodist Church
traditions.summary: Methodism reached Korea with American missionaries Henry Appenzeller and William Scranton in 1885. In 1930 the northern and southern American Methodist missions united to form the autonomous Korean Methodist Church. Korean Methodists were prominent in the 1919 independence movement, and the church grew dramatically after the Korean War.

profile.authority: Scripture with Methodist doctrinal standards and Korean confessional statements.
profile.salvation: Wesleyan: universal grace and sanctification.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and Holy Communion.
profile.eschatology: Classical hope of Christ's return.
profile.governance: Episcopal with bishops elected for set terms.
profile.worship: Methodist liturgy with Korean revival prayer practices.

traditions.status: Active; one of the largest Methodist churches in Asia.

traditions.name: Church of God in Christ
traditions.summary: Founded in 1897 in Mississippi by Charles Harrison Mason and Charles Price Jones as a holiness church. After Mason received Spirit baptism at the Azusa Street revival in 1907, the church divided; Mason's Pentecostal majority kept the name, and Jones's group became the Church of Christ (Holiness). For years COGIC was one of the few incorporated Pentecostal bodies able to ordain clergy, including many white ministers. Headquartered in Memphis, it is the largest Pentecostal denomination in the United States and a pillar of African American church life; Martin Luther King Jr. gave his final 'Mountaintop' speech at its Mason Temple in 1968.
distinctives: Black-led church founded by former slaves' children
Women's Department as a powerful parallel structure

profile.authority: Scripture as inspired Word; COGIC Official Manual.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith, sanctification and baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and feet washing as ordinances.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial return of Christ.
profile.governance: Episcopal: Presiding Bishop, General Board, jurisdictional bishops; women serve as evangelists and missionaries but not as pastors or bishops.
profile.worship: Ecstatic worship with shouting, tarrying, testimony and gospel choirs.

traditions.status: Active; one of the largest Pentecostal bodies in North America.

traditions.name: Church of God (Cleveland, Tennessee)
traditions.summary: Traces its origins to the Christian Union formed by Richard Spurling at Barney Creek, Tennessee, in 1886, and the 1896 Shearer Schoolhouse revival in North Carolina. Under A. J. Tomlinson it became Pentecostal after G. B. Cashwell, back from Azusa Street, preached in Cleveland in 1908. A 1923 dispute led to Tomlinson's Church of God of Prophecy. Now a large worldwide church.
distinctives: Oldest Pentecostal denomination in the U.S. by founding date

profile.authority: Scripture as the Word of God, "rightly divided"; Declaration of Faith (1948).
profile.salvation: Justification, sanctification and baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and feet washing.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial second coming.
profile.governance: Centralised: General Assembly and General Overseer appoint state overseers.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship.

traditions.status: Active; worldwide membership in the millions.

traditions.name: International Church of the Foursquare Gospel
traditions.summary: Founded by the evangelist Aimee Semple McPherson, who opened Angelus Temple in Los Angeles in 1923 and incorporated the denomination in 1927. A pioneer of religious radio and of social relief during the Depression, she preached the 'Foursquare Gospel' of Jesus as Saviour, Baptiser with the Holy Spirit, Healer and Coming King.
distinctives: Founded and led by a woman
Foursquare Gospel (adapted from A. B. Simpson)
Early use of radio and dramatic sermons
Strong in Brazil, the Philippines and Nigeria

profile.authority: Scripture; the Declaration of Faith written by McPherson.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith; Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial return of Christ.
profile.governance: Central board and president with district supervisors.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship with contemporary music.

traditions.status: Active internationally.

traditions.name: The Apostolic Church
traditions.summary: A Pentecostal church formed in 1916 at Penygroes, Carmarthenshire, by Daniel Powell Williams, a convert of the 1904–05 Welsh Revival. It recognises the present-day offices of apostle and prophet (Ephesians 4:11) and gives a central place to directive prophecy in church government. Its missions made it large in Nigeria and Ghana.
distinctives: Restored offices of apostle and prophet

profile.authority: Scripture as final authority, with prophetic guidance in church affairs tested by it.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace; Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial return of Christ.
profile.governance: Government by apostles and prophets with elders and deacons.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship with prophecy.

traditions.status: Active; largest branches in Nigeria and Ghana.

traditions.name: Elim Pentecostal Church
traditions.summary: Founded in Monaghan, Ireland, in 1915 by the Welsh evangelist George Jeffreys, whose healing campaigns filled the Royal Albert Hall in the 1920s–30s. Elim became one of the main British Pentecostal denominations; Jeffreys left in 1940 over church government. In 1978 missionaries and their families were murdered at an Elim mission in Rhodesia (Vumba).
distinctives: More centralised than British Assemblies of God
Does not require tongues as the only initial evidence

profile.authority: Scripture as infallible; Elim Fundamental Truths.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace; Spirit baptism with signs following.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial return of Christ.
profile.governance: Connexional, with a General Conference and central leadership.
profile.worship: Pentecostal and contemporary worship.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Pentecostal Assemblies of the World
traditions.summary: Organised in Los Angeles about 1907 and reorganised in 1918 as an interracial Oneness body after merging with the General Assembly of Apostolic Assemblies; Garfield T. Haywood, an African American pastor in Indianapolis, became its first Presiding Bishop in 1925. Most white ministers withdrew in 1924, forming bodies that later became the United Pentecostal Church. It stands outside historic Nicene Trinitarian orthodoxy.
distinctives: Oneness theology: one God revealed as Father, Son and Spirit, whose name is Jesus
Baptism in the name of Jesus

profile.authority: Scripture; rejects the Nicene doctrine of three persons as unbiblical.
profile.salvation: Repentance, baptism in Jesus' name and Spirit baptism with tongues (Acts 2:38) as the new birth.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord's Supper and feet washing.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial return of Christ.
profile.governance: Episcopal: Presiding Bishop and diocesan bishops.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: United Pentecostal Church International
traditions.summary: The largest Oneness Pentecostal denomination, formed in St Louis in 1945 by the merger of the Pentecostal Church, Inc. and the Pentecostal Assemblies of Jesus Christ. It teaches that the one God is fully revealed in Jesus Christ and that baptism in Jesus' name and the gift of tongues are part of the new birth. It stands outside historic Nicene Trinitarianism.
distinctives: Acts 2:38 as the plan of salvation
Strict holiness standards of dress and appearance
Large missions in Latin America and the Philippines

profile.authority: Scripture as the inspired Word; rejects Trinitarian creeds.
profile.salvation: Repentance, water baptism in Jesus' name and Spirit baptism with tongues.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion in Jesus' name, the Lord's Supper and feet washing.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial rapture and return of Christ.
profile.governance: Congregational churches with a General Conference and General Superintendent.
profile.worship: Exuberant Pentecostal worship.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Assembleias de Deus (Brazil)
traditions.summary: Founded in Belém in 1911 by the Swedish missionaries Daniel Berg and Gunnar Vingren, after their Pentecostal teaching led to expulsion from a Baptist church. Linked historically with Swedish rather than U.S. Pentecostalism, the Assemblies of God in Brazil grew into the country's largest Protestant family, now divided among several large conventions and ministries.
distinctives: Strict traditional usos e costumes in many congregations
Growing political influence in Brazil's evangelical caucus

profile.authority: Scripture; Declaration of Faith of the CGADB.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith; Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial, pre-tribulation rapture.
profile.governance: Mother churches (ministérios) with pastor-presidents and networks of dependent congregations; national conventions.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship.

traditions.status: Active; the largest Pentecostal family in Brazil.

traditions.name: Yoido Full Gospel Church
traditions.summary: Begun as a tent church in a Seoul slum in 1958 by David Yonggi Cho and Choi Ja-shil, affiliated with the Assemblies of God. Moving to Yeouido island in 1973, it became the largest single congregation in the world, organised around home cell groups. Cho's 'threefold blessing' (spiritual, physical and material well-being, from 3 John 2) has been criticised as a prosperity gospel; Cho was also convicted of embezzlement in 2014.

profile.authority: Scripture; Assemblies of God doctrine.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace; Spirit baptism; healing and blessing as fruits of the gospel.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial return of Christ.
profile.governance: Senior pastor with elders and cell leaders; affiliated with the Korean Assemblies of God.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship, all-night and early-morning prayer.

traditions.status: Active; membership reported in the hundreds of thousands.

traditions.name: Redeemed Christian Church of God
traditions.summary: Founded in Lagos in 1952 by Josiah Akindayomi, who had belonged to the Cherubim and Seraphim. Under Enoch Adejare Adeboye (General Overseer from 1981) it became a Pentecostal megachurch movement planting 'parishes' worldwide, known for the Holy Ghost Congress at Redemption Camp on the Lagos–Ibadan expressway.
distinctives: Strong diaspora presence in Britain and North America

profile.authority: Scripture; the General Overseer's teaching highly influential.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace, holiness and Spirit baptism.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion, the Lord's Supper and feet washing in some parishes.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial rapture and return of Christ.
profile.governance: Hierarchical: General Overseer, regional and provincial pastors.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship with all-night prayer.

traditions.status: Active in many countries.

traditions.name: Universal Church of the Kingdom of God
traditions.summary: Founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1977 by Edir Macedo. A neo-Pentecostal church emphasising deliverance from evil spirits, healing and prosperity through sacrificial giving, it built the vast Temple of Solomon in São Paulo (2014), owns the RecordTV network and is linked to the Republicanos party. It has faced investigations and conflicts in several countries (e.g. the 2019–21 schism and expulsion of Brazilian bishops in Angola), which the church contests; critics also cite hostility to Afro-Brazilian religions.
distinctives: Deliverance sessions confronting spirits (often identified with Afro-Brazilian deities)

profile.authority: Scripture as interpreted by the church's leadership.
profile.salvation: Faith in Christ expressed through sacrifice and confrontation of evil; healing and prosperity as signs.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return; little emphasis compared with present deliverance.
profile.governance: Centralised episcopal hierarchy under the founding bishop.
profile.worship: Daily themed services (prosperity, healing, family, deliverance).

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Vineyard Churches
traditions.summary: A movement begun with Kenneth Gulliksen's Vineyard Fellowship (1974) and shaped from 1982 by John Wimber, a former Calvary Chapel pastor. Wimber taught 'power evangelism' and the 'Third Wave' of the Spirit, combining evangelical theology with healing and prophecy while avoiding Pentecostal labels. The Vineyard released the Toronto Airport congregation in 1995 over the 'Toronto Blessing'. Vineyard worship songs shaped global contemporary worship.
distinctives: Kingdom theology (George Eldon Ladd's 'already and not yet')
'Everyone gets to play' — ministry by all believers

profile.authority: Scripture as the final authority; Vineyard Statement of Faith.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith; ongoing filling of the Spirit without tongues as required evidence.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Inaugurated kingdom eschatology.
profile.governance: Association of churches with national movements; senior pastors.
profile.worship: Extended intimate worship followed by teaching and ministry time.

traditions.status: Active internationally.

traditions.name: Calvary Chapel
traditions.summary: Began when Chuck Smith, formerly a Foursquare pastor, took over a small church in Costa Mesa, California, in 1965 and welcomed hippies of the Jesus Movement with the help of Lonnie Frisbee. It pioneered contemporary Christian music (Maranatha! Music), verse-by-verse Bible teaching and mass beach baptisms. Calvary Chapel describes itself as a middle way between fundamentalism and Pentecostal emotionalism.

profile.authority: Scripture as inerrant; no denominational confession beyond Calvary Chapel distinctives.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith.
profile.sacraments: Believers' baptism (often in the ocean) and communion.
profile.eschatology: Pre-tribulation rapture, premillennial return.
profile.governance: Senior pastor with board; loose fellowship of affiliated churches (two associations since 2016).
profile.worship: Contemporary worship with Bible teaching.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Hillsong Church
traditions.summary: Founded in 1983 as Hills Christian Life Centre in Sydney by Brian and Bobbie Houston within the Assemblies of God in Australia; renamed Hillsong in 1999. Its worship music became among the most widely sung in the world, and it planted large churches in global cities. It left the Australian Christian Churches in 2018. From 2020 scandals involving leaders led to the departure of many campuses and Brian Houston's resignation (2022); he was acquitted in 2023 of concealing his father's abuse.
distinctives: Pentecostal theology with polished contemporary presentation

profile.authority: Scripture; Pentecostal statement of faith.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace; Spirit-filled life and flourishing.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and communion.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return.
profile.governance: Global senior pastors with a board.
profile.worship: Concert-style worship with professional music production.

traditions.status: Active; reduced after 2020–22 crises.

traditions.name: Bethel Church (Redding) and New Apostolic Reformation networks
traditions.summary: A loose constellation of independent charismatic networks led by self-described apostles and prophets. C. Peter Wagner popularised the term 'New Apostolic Reformation' in the 1990s for what he saw as the restoration of apostolic governance. Bethel Church in Redding, California, led by Bill Johnson since 1996, left the Assemblies of God in 2006 and became influential through its supernatural ministry school and worship music. Many participants reject the NAR label; critics raise concerns about extra-biblical revelation and the political 'Seven Mountains' mandate.
distinctives: 'Kingdom now' theology of heaven invading earth

profile.authority: Scripture as final authority, with emphasis on ongoing prophetic revelation.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace; believers called to exercise supernatural power.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and communion.
profile.eschatology: Optimistic, often victorious or postmillennial-leaning eschatology.
profile.governance: Relational apostolic networks without formal denominational structures.
profile.worship: Long worship sets, prophetic ministry and healing prayer.

traditions.status: Active; widely influential and debated.

traditions.name: Kimbanguist Church (EJCSK)
traditions.summary: The Church of Jesus Christ on Earth through the Prophet Simon Kimbangu traces its origin to Kimbangu's healing ministry at Nkamba in the Belgian Congo in 1921. Arrested within months, Kimbangu died in prison in 1951 while his followers were deported and persecuted. The church was legally recognised in 1959, joined the World Council of Churches in 1969 and is among Africa's largest independent churches. Later teaching that exalted Simon Kimbangu and his successors, including identification of Kimbangu with the Holy Spirit, has strained relations with other Congolese Protestant churches.
distinctives: Strict ethics: no alcohol, tobacco, pork or violence

profile.authority: Scripture, with the revelations of Simon Kimbangu and his successors.
profile.salvation: Salvation in Christ, mediated through obedience and the prophetic ministry.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by laying on of hands (without water) and communion with locally produced elements.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of judgment and renewal centred on the holy city of Nkamba.
profile.governance: Spiritual heads drawn from Kimbangu's family.
profile.worship: Brass bands, choirs, prayers and pilgrimage to Nkamba.

traditions.status: Active; millions of adherents in the DRC and neighbouring countries.

traditions.name: Zion Christian Church
traditions.summary: Founded by Engenas Lekganyane about 1924 in the northern Transvaal, from the 'Zionist' movement that grew from the Christian Catholic Church of John Alexander Dowie (Zion, Illinois) through South African leaders. The ZCC, headquartered at Moria in Limpopo, is the largest church in southern Africa; its Easter pilgrimage draws over a million people. It combines Christian faith with healing through blessed water and other objects and with African ways of life.
distinctives: Healing through prayer, blessed water, tea and cords
Star and dove badges worn by members
Prohibition of alcohol, tobacco and pork

profile.authority: Scripture as read and applied by the bishop.
profile.salvation: Salvation and healing in Christ, protection from evil and wholeness of life.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by triple immersion and Holy Communion.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of God's Kingdom; focus on present wellbeing.
profile.governance: Hereditary bishop with ministers and preachers.
profile.worship: Dancing, singing, uniforms and testimony; pilgrimage.

traditions.status: Active; the largest independent church in southern Africa.

traditions.name: Church of the Lord (Aladura)
traditions.summary: Founded in 1930 at Ogere, Nigeria, by Josiah Olunowo Ositelu, a former Anglican catechist who received visions. One of the Yoruba 'praying' (Aladura) churches, it uses prayer, fasting, holy names and prophecy for healing and protection, and spread to Ghana, Liberia, Sierra Leone and Britain. It joined the World Council of Churches in 1975.
distinctives: Prayer as central practice (aladura = "owners of prayer")
Holy names and sacred seals revealed to the founder

profile.authority: Scripture with revelations given to the founder and prophets.
profile.salvation: Salvation in Christ, experienced as healing, protection and power through prayer.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and Holy Communion.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return.
profile.governance: Primate and hierarchy of bishops, prophets and apostles.
profile.worship: White-robed worship, barefoot, with drumming, prayer and ecstatic prophecy.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Celestial Church of Christ
traditions.summary: Founded at Porto-Novo, Dahomey (now Benin), in 1947 by Samuel Bilewu Oshoffa after a vision during an eclipse. A prophetic-healing church related to the Aladura family, it spread rapidly in Nigeria and the West African diaspora. Members worship in white garments, barefoot, and observe purity rules.
distinctives: Visions and prophecy guiding church life
White soutanes and bare feet in worship
Rejection of traditional charms and idols

profile.authority: Scripture with the revelations given to the founder.
profile.salvation: Salvation in Christ, protection from evil, healing.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and Holy Communion.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of Christ's return.
profile.governance: Pastor-founder succeeded by Pastors; hierarchy of ranks.
profile.worship: Liturgy with chanting, candles, incense and prophetic visions.

traditions.status: Active; succession disputes have produced rival factions since 1985.

traditions.name: Nazareth Baptist Church (amaNazaretha / Shembe)
traditions.summary: Founded in 1910 in Natal by the Zulu prophet Isaiah Shembe, who had been associated with the African Native Baptist Church. Centred on the holy village of Ekuphakameni and the mountain Nhlangakazi, it blends biblical faith with Zulu culture and Sabbath observance. Many members regard Shembe as a divinely sent prophet or messianic figure, a view outsiders and members interpret differently. It has divided among Shembe's descendants.

profile.authority: Scripture, especially the Old Testament, with the hymns and revelations of the Shembe prophets.
profile.salvation: Salvation through God revealed in Christ and in the prophet Shembe.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and Holy Communion (including a night communion with feet washing).
profile.eschatology: Expectation of judgment and divine restoration.
profile.governance: Leadership by successors of Isaiah Shembe.
profile.worship: Hymn-singing and sacred dance on Sabbath and festivals.

traditions.status: Active; several factions.

traditions.name: Harrist Church
traditions.summary: Communities formed in Côte d'Ivoire by converts of the Liberian prophet William Wade Harris (1913–15), who baptised tens of thousands and told them to wait for 'teachers with Bibles'. Many joined the Methodist mission; others organised under John Ahui, whom Harris commissioned in 1928, into the Harrist Church, officially recognised in the 1950s.
distinctives: Founder's call to burn fetishes and turn to the one God

profile.authority: Scripture as proclaimed by Harris; oral tradition of his teaching.
profile.salvation: Turning to God and away from idols, with baptism.
profile.sacraments: Baptism; communion not central.
profile.eschatology: Expectation of judgment.
profile.governance: Preachers and apostles with a central council.
profile.worship: Singing in local languages and preaching in white robes.

traditions.status: Active in Côte d'Ivoire.

traditions.name: Iglesia ni Cristo
traditions.summary: A Filipino church registered in 1914 by Felix Y. Manalo, who had been a member of several Protestant churches including the Seventh-day Adventists. It teaches that the original church apostatised and was re-established through Manalo as God's last messenger. It rejects the Trinity, holding that Jesus is the Son of God and Saviour but not God, and so stands outside historic Nicene Christianity. It is noted for disciplined membership, monumental chapels and bloc voting.
distinctives: Membership in the INC necessary for salvation

profile.authority: Scripture as interpreted by the church's Executive Minister.
profile.salvation: Salvation through membership in the true Church of Christ and obedience.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and the Holy Supper (annual).
profile.eschatology: Judgment Day with salvation for faithful members.
profile.governance: Centralised under the Executive Minister.
profile.worship: Twice-weekly worship with doctrinal sermons and choirs.

traditions.status: Active; large in the Philippines and the Filipino diaspora.

traditions.name: True Jesus Church
traditions.summary: An independent Chinese church founded in Beijing in 1917 by Paul Wei (Wei Enbo) and others, combining Oneness Pentecostal theology with Saturday Sabbath observance. It holds itself to be the restored true church. Strong in Taiwan and among Chinese communities worldwide, it was absorbed into the Three-Self structure on the mainland but continues independently elsewhere.
distinctives: Baptism by face-down immersion in natural water in Jesus' name

profile.authority: Scripture as the only basis; claims restored apostolic church.
profile.salvation: Salvation requires baptism, Spirit baptism with tongues and keeping the Sabbath.
profile.sacraments: Water baptism, feet washing and Holy Communion.
profile.eschatology: Return of Christ.
profile.governance: Councils of elders and ministers.
profile.worship: Prayer in tongues together, preaching and hymns.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Local Churches (Watchman Nee and Witness Lee)
traditions.summary: A Chinese church movement that began in Fuzhou in the early 1920s around Watchman Nee, influenced by the Brethren and Keswick teaching, holding that there should be one church per city. Nee was imprisoned by the Communist government from 1952 until his death in 1972. Witness Lee carried the movement to Taiwan (1949) and the United States (1962). Some evangelical critics accused Lee's teachings of modalism and other errors; the Christian Research Institute retracted its earlier criticism in 2009, though others still dissent.
distinctives: Inner life and the spirit (Nee's The Normal Christian Life)
'Calling on the name of the Lord' and 'pray-reading' Scripture

profile.authority: Scripture, read through the ministry of Watchman Nee and Witness Lee.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace and the dispensing of the divine life into believers.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and the Lord's table.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial; the overcomers and the kingdom.
profile.governance: Elders in each local church; no denominational office.
profile.worship: Mutual participation, calling on the Lord and pray-reading.

traditions.status: Active in China (often unregistered), Taiwan and elsewhere.

traditions.name: Three-Self Patriotic Movement and China Christian Council
traditions.summary: The state-registered Protestant church structure of the People's Republic of China, based on the 'three-self' principles (self-government, self-support, self-propagation) of earlier missionary thinking. Formalised in 1954 under Y. T. Wu after the 1950 Christian Manifesto cut ties with foreign missions, it imposed post-denominational unity. Suspended during the Cultural Revolution, it was restored in 1979, with the China Christian Council formed in 1980 under Bishop K. H. Ting. Unregistered house churches reject its accommodation to state control; supporters see it as the legal space that allowed churches to reopen.
distinctives: Registration with the state Religious Affairs authorities

profile.authority: Scripture; preaching expected to accord with state regulations on religion.
profile.salvation: Protestant evangelical faith in Christ in varied forms.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper in forms from former denominations.
profile.eschatology: Varied; apocalyptic preaching discouraged.
profile.governance: Two national bodies (TSPM and CCC) with provincial councils, under state oversight.
profile.worship: Sunday services in registered churches, often crowded.

traditions.status: Active; tens of millions of members in registered churches.

traditions.name: Jesus Family
traditions.summary: A communal Pentecostal-style Christian community founded by Jing Dianying, a former Methodist, at Mazhuang, Shandong, in 1927. Members pooled property, worked the land together and practised ecstatic worship. It spread to over a hundred communities before the Communist government dissolved it in 1952.
distinctives: Care for the poor and disabled

profile.authority: Scripture with revelations in visions and dreams.
profile.salvation: Salvation by faith expressed in total self-giving to the community.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Strong expectation of Christ's imminent return.
profile.governance: Patriarchal leader (Jing Dianying) with elders.
profile.worship: Ecstatic worship and communal labour.

traditions.status: Historic; dissolved 1952, though its influence persisted in house churches.

traditions.name: Indian Pentecostal Church of God
traditions.summary: Founded in Kerala in 1924 by K. E. Abraham and others who sought Indian leadership independent of foreign missionaries.
