Drawing many converts from Syrian Christian (Mar Thoma and Orthodox) and Dalit communities, it became one of the largest indigenous Pentecostal churches in India.
distinctives: Strong in Kerala and the Gulf diaspora
Plain dress and no jewellery in many congregations

profile.authority: Scripture as inerrant.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace; Baptism in the Holy Spirit as an experience subsequent to conversion, usually evidenced by speaking in tongues; gifts of healing and prophecy for today.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial, pre-tribulation rapture.
profile.governance: Central council with state councils.
profile.worship: Pentecostal worship in Malayalam and other languages.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Churches of Christ (a cappella)
traditions.summary: Congregations of the Stone-Campbell movement that separated from the Disciples of Christ, recognised in the 1906 U.S. Religious Census. Reading the New Testament as a pattern for the church, they reject instrumental music in worship and organisations beyond the local congregation as unauthorised by Scripture. They see themselves not as a denomination but as the restored New Testament church.
distinctives: Baptism by immersion for the forgiveness of sins
Autonomous congregations with no denominational headquarters
'Speak where the Bible speaks, be silent where the Bible is silent'

profile.authority: The New Testament as the pattern for faith and practice: command, example and necessary inference; no creeds.
profile.salvation: Hearing, believing, repenting, confessing Christ and being immersed for the remission of sins; faithful living.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion of penitent believers and the Lord's Supper every Sunday.
profile.eschatology: Mostly amillennial; Christ's return and judgment.
profile.governance: Autonomous congregations led by elders and deacons; no clergy hierarchy.
profile.worship: Unaccompanied singing, weekly communion and preaching.

traditions.status: Active; non-institutional and other sub-fellowships exist.

traditions.name: Christian Church (Disciples of Christ)
traditions.summary: The ecumenical, mainline branch of the Stone-Campbell movement, dating its unity to the 1832 union of Barton Stone's 'Christians' and Alexander Campbell's 'Disciples'. After the Churches of Christ separated (1906) and the independent Christian Churches drifted away, it restructured as a denomination in 1968. It practises open weekly communion and was a founding member of the World Council of Churches; in 2005 Sharon Watkins became the first woman to lead a U.S. mainline denomination.
distinctives: Weekly open communion at the centre of worship
Commitment to Christian unity (Council on Christian Unity)
Ecumenical partnership with the United Church of Christ (1989)

profile.authority: Scripture and the confession that Jesus is the Christ; freedom of interpretation.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
profile.sacraments: Believer's baptism by immersion, with members received from other churches; the Lord's Supper weekly, open to all.
profile.eschatology: Varied; mainstream Christian hope.
profile.governance: Congregational with regions and a General Assembly (restructure 1968).
profile.worship: Lay elders preside at the table alongside ordained ministers.

traditions.status: Active; declining membership typical of mainline churches.

traditions.name: Christian Churches and Churches of Christ (independent)
traditions.summary: Independent congregations of the Stone-Campbell movement, theologically conservative and using instrumental music, that distanced themselves from the Disciples over liberal theology, open membership and denominational structures. The North American Christian Convention (1927) gave them a forum, and they were listed separately from the Disciples by 1971. Many large evangelical megachurches belong to this fellowship.

profile.authority: Scripture as inerrant; no creed.
profile.salvation: Faith, repentance and immersion as the response to the gospel.
profile.sacraments: Believers' immersion and weekly Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Varied, often premillennial.
profile.governance: Autonomous congregations led by elders.
profile.worship: Contemporary evangelical worship with weekly communion.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Community of Christ (formerly RLDS Church)
traditions.summary: The Reorganized Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, organised by Latter Day Saints who rejected Brigham Young's leadership and polygamy; Joseph Smith III became its prophet-president at Amboy, Illinois, in 1860. Headquartered in Independence, Missouri, it has moved toward mainstream Protestant theology: it ordains women (1984), practises open communion (1994), affirms the Trinity, and treats the Book of Mormon as scripture without making it a test of faithfulness. Renamed in 2001.
distinctives: Ongoing revelation added to its Doctrine and Covenants
Temple in Independence dedicated to peace (1994)
Mission focused on peace and justice
Never practised polygamy as a church

profile.authority: Scripture (Bible) with the Book of Mormon and its Doctrine and Covenants, interpreted through Christ and continuing revelation through the prophet-president.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, expressed in discipleship and community.
profile.sacraments: Eight sacraments: baptism, confirmation, Lord's Supper, marriage, blessing of children, ordination, laying on of hands for the sick and evangelist blessing.
profile.eschatology: Hope for the peaceable kingdom (Zion) on earth.
profile.governance: Prophet-president, First Presidency, Council of Twelve and World Conference.
profile.worship: Protestant-style worship with communion.
profile.canon: The Bible, the Book of Mormon and the Community of Christ Doctrine and Covenants.

traditions.status: Active; a few hundred thousand members worldwide.

traditions.name: Christadelphians
traditions.summary: A lay movement founded by John Thomas, an English-born physician in the Campbell movement who was re-immersed in 1847 after concluding that baptism must follow understanding of the gospel of the Kingdom. The name 'Christadelphians' ('brothers in Christ') was adopted in 1864 to register as conscientious objectors during the U.S. Civil War. Robert Roberts of Birmingham organised the British ecclesias. They reject the Trinity, the pre-existence of Christ and the immortality of the soul, standing outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
distinctives: One God, the Father; Jesus the Son of God, not pre-existent
Holy Spirit as God's power, not a person
Mortality of the soul and resurrection at Christ's return
Kingdom of God on earth centred on Israel

profile.authority: Scripture alone, interpreted through the Birmingham Amended Statement of Faith (1898) in many ecclesias.
profile.salvation: Belief of the gospel of the Kingdom and the name of Jesus, followed by immersion, and a faithful life.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion of informed believers and weekly breaking of bread.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial: Christ will return to raise and judge the responsible and reign from Jerusalem; the wicked perish.
profile.governance: Autonomous ecclesias with elected arranging brethren.
profile.worship: Simple memorial meeting and Bible exposition.

traditions.status: Active; ecclesias worldwide.

traditions.name: Church of Christ, Scientist
traditions.summary: Founded in Boston in 1879 by Mary Baker Eddy, raised a New England Congregationalist, following her recovery from injury in 1866 and her book Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures (1875). It teaches that God is wholly good, infinite Mind, and that matter, sin and disease are not ultimately real, so healing comes through spiritual understanding rather than medicine. It reinterprets the Trinity and stands outside historic Nicene Christianity. It published the Christian Science Monitor (1908).
distinctives: Spiritual healing through prayer and Christian Science practitioners
Science and Health as the "pastor" alongside the Bible
No ordained clergy; readers lead services

profile.authority: The Bible and Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures as the impersonal pastor.
profile.salvation: Salvation as awakening from the belief in matter, sin and death through understanding of God as Mind and Love.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and communion understood spiritually, without water or elements.
profile.eschatology: Salvation realised through spiritual progress; no physical second coming emphasis.
profile.governance: The Mother Church governed by a Board of Directors under the Church Manual.
profile.worship: Sunday Lesson-Sermons read from the Bible and Science and Health; Wednesday testimony meetings.
profile.canon: The Bible with Science and Health.

traditions.status: Active but much declined since the mid-twentieth century.

traditions.name: Unity (Unity Church / Unity School of Christianity)
traditions.summary: A New Thought movement founded in Kansas City in 1889 by Charles and Myrtle Fillmore after Myrtle's healing, influenced by Emma Curtis Hopkins (a former student of Mary Baker Eddy). Unity teaches the divinity in every person, affirmative prayer and the power of thought; it is known for the Silent Unity prayer ministry and the Daily Word. It stands outside historic Christian orthodoxy.
distinctives: Jesus as the great example of the indwelling Christ

profile.authority: Scripture read metaphysically, with spiritual experience.
profile.salvation: Realisation of the Christ within; no doctrine of eternal punishment.
profile.sacraments: No formal sacraments; symbolic baptism and communion in some congregations.
profile.eschatology: Present spiritual realisation; reincarnation accepted by many.
profile.governance: Unity Worldwide Ministries association of congregations; Unity World Headquarters at Unity Village.
profile.worship: Meditation, affirmations and talks.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Shakers (United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing)
traditions.summary: Emerged about 1747 near Manchester among followers of James and Jane Wardley, influenced by Quakers and French Camisard prophets. Ann Lee led a group to America in 1774; under Joseph Meacham and Lucy Wright the Shakers built celibate communal villages from Maine to Kentucky. Many Believers regarded Ann Lee as the female appearing of the Christ spirit. Known for ecstatic dance, gender equality in leadership, craftsmanship and songs like 'Simple Gifts'. Only Sabbathday Lake, Maine, remains, with a handful of members.

profile.authority: Scripture with ongoing revelation and the testimony of Ann Lee and early leaders.
profile.salvation: Salvation through confession, celibacy and a life of separation from the world.
profile.sacraments: No outward sacraments.
profile.eschatology: Christ's second appearing understood as already begun in the Believers.
profile.governance: Ministry of elders and eldresses in each family and a central ministry.
profile.worship: Song and dance, later quieter meetings.

traditions.status: Nearly extinct: one community at Sabbathday Lake, Maine.

traditions.name: New Church (Swedenborgian)
traditions.summary: Churches based on the visionary writings of the Swedish scientist Emanuel Swedenborg (1688–1772), who taught that the Last Judgment occurred in the spiritual world in 1757 and that the Lord had opened the inner sense of Scripture. The first New Church society was organised in London in 1787. Swedenborgians teach that God is one in essence and person, Jesus Christ, in whom there is a trinity of love, wisdom and operation, rather than three persons; they therefore stand outside Nicene Trinitarianism as historically defined.
distinctives: Revelation through Swedenborg of the spiritual sense of the Word
One God in one Person, the Lord Jesus Christ
Life of charity as essential to salvation
Detailed teaching on heaven, hell and the spiritual world
Influence on figures such as Blake, Emerson and Helen Keller

profile.authority: The Word in its spiritual sense, as unfolded in Swedenborg's Writings.
profile.salvation: Regeneration through faith joined to charity and useful life; no vicarious satisfaction.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Holy Supper.
profile.eschatology: The Last Judgment occurred in 1757; the Second Coming is the revelation of the inner sense of Scripture; the New Jerusalem is descending.
profile.governance: Several bodies: General Conference (UK), General Convention (US, 1817) and the episcopally led General Church (Bryn Athyn).
profile.worship: Liturgical worship.
profile.canon: The 'Word' as Swedenborg defined it (books with an internal sense), with the other biblical books valued as edifying.

traditions.status: Active but small.

traditions.name: Bible Students (Independent)
traditions.summary: Fellowships that continue Charles Taze Russell's original Bible Student movement (from 1879) and separated from the Watch Tower Society after J. F. Rutherford took control in 1917. Bodies such as the Pastoral Bible Institute (1918) and the Dawn Bible Students remain loyal to Russell's Studies in the Scriptures, rejecting Rutherford's centralisation. They share the movement's non-Trinitarian theology and stand outside historic Nicene orthodoxy.
distinctives: Ransom and restitution: a future opportunity for all humanity
Rejection of eternal torment and the Trinity

profile.authority: Scripture, read through Russell's Studies in the Scriptures.
profile.salvation: Salvation through the ransom of Christ; most of humanity will receive an opportunity in the Millennial age.
profile.sacraments: Immersion of consecrated believers and the annual Memorial of Christ's death.
profile.eschatology: Millennial restitution of mankind on earth; a heavenly 'little flock' of 144,000.
profile.governance: Independent ecclesias with elected elders.
profile.worship: Bible studies, testimony meetings and conventions.

traditions.status: Active but small.

traditions.name: Church of God (Seventh Day)
traditions.summary: Sabbath-keeping Adventists, led initially by Gilbert Cranmer in Michigan (1858), who declined to follow Ellen G. White's prophetic authority or the name 'Seventh-day Adventist'. Organised as a General Conference in 1884 and later based in Denver, it experienced a 1933 schism (Salem, West Virginia). Historically non-Trinitarian (often binitarian), with views varying among its bodies; Herbert W. Armstrong came from its Oregon conference.
distinctives: Rejection of Ellen G. White's writings as authoritative
Annual Lord's Supper on Passover evening
Name "Church of God" as the biblical name

profile.authority: Scripture alone.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith, with obedience to God's commandments including the Sabbath.
profile.sacraments: Baptism by immersion and the annual Lord's Supper with feet washing.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial return of Christ; resurrection and annihilation of the wicked.
profile.governance: General Conference with ministerial council.
profile.worship: Saturday worship.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: Worldwide Church of God (Armstrong era)
traditions.summary: Founded as the Radio Church of God in 1933 in Eugene, Oregon, by Herbert W. Armstrong, a former Church of God (Seventh Day) minister, later headquartered in Pasadena with Ambassador College and The Plain Truth magazine. It taught Sabbath and Old Testament holy days, tithing, British Israelism and a binitarian 'God Family' that believers would join. After Armstrong's death it renounced these teachings (1993–97) and became Grace Communion International in 2009.
distinctives: Seventh-day Sabbath and annual holy days
Mass media evangelism (The World Tomorrow broadcast)

profile.authority: Scripture as interpreted by Armstrong as God's apostle.
profile.salvation: Obedience to God's law with Christ's sacrifice; believers to be born into the God Family at the resurrection.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and annual Passover.
profile.eschatology: Imminent end-time tribulation and the World Tomorrow.
profile.governance: Hierarchical under the Pastor General.
profile.worship: Saturday services and holy-day festivals.

traditions.status: Historic as described; transformed into Grace Communion International, while splinter groups continue Armstrong's teaching.

traditions.name: Grace Communion International
traditions.summary: The former Worldwide Church of God, which under Joseph W. Tkach and his son Joseph Tkach Jr. rejected Armstrong's distinctive teachings, embraced the Trinity and salvation by grace, joined the National Association of Evangelicals (1997) and took a new name in 2009. Its theology is now strongly 'Trinitarian-incarnational', drawing on Karl Barth and T. F. and J. B. Torrance.
distinctives: Salvation by grace without Old Covenant law

profile.authority: Scripture, read in harmony with the historic creeds.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through Christ, who has included humanity in his life with the Father in the Spirit.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Christ's return and the reconciliation of all things in him; universalism not taught as dogma.
profile.governance: Denominational leadership with national churches.
profile.worship: Sunday evangelical worship.

traditions.name: Messianic Judaism
traditions.summary: A movement of Jewish people (and non-Jewish associates) who believe Jesus (Yeshua) is the Messiah while retaining Jewish identity and practice. It grew from nineteenth-century Hebrew Christian associations; the Hebrew Christian Alliance of America (1915) renamed itself the Messianic Jewish Alliance of America in 1975, and the Union of Messianic Jewish Congregations followed in 1979. Mainstream Jewish bodies and Israeli courts generally do not regard Messianic Jews as Jews, and many see the movement as a form of Christian missionising; Messianic Jews regard faith in Yeshua as the fulfilment of Judaism.
distinctives: Observance of Sabbath and Jewish festivals
Jewish identity affirmed after faith in Yeshua
Congregations in Israel and the diaspora

profile.authority: Hebrew Bible and New Testament (Brit Hadashah); Jewish tradition valued in varying degrees.
profile.salvation: Salvation through Yeshua the Messiah, for Jew and Gentile.
profile.sacraments: Immersion (mikveh) of believers; the Lord's Supper often linked with Passover.
profile.eschatology: Premillennial, with a central place for Israel.
profile.governance: Congregational with rabbis and elders; unions of congregations.
profile.worship: Sabbath services with Torah reading, Hebrew prayers and Davidic dance.
profile.canon: The Hebrew Bible and the New Testament.

traditions.status: Active and debated.

traditions.name: Church of South India
traditions.summary: Formed on 27 September 1947 at St George's Cathedral, Madras, by the union of Anglican dioceses, the Methodist Church of South India and the South India United Church (Presbyterian and Congregational). It was the first union of episcopal and non-episcopal churches, accepting the historic episcopate while recognising existing ministries without reordination. It has been a leading voice for Dalit Christians, who form a majority of its members.
distinctives: First union of episcopal and non-episcopal churches
CSI Liturgy (1950s) influential on liturgical renewal worldwide
Full communion with Anglicans, Methodists and Reformed

profile.authority: Scripture as the supreme standard, with the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (infants and believers) and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Classical Christian hope.
profile.governance: Episcopal-synodical: dioceses with bishops, a Synod and Moderator.
profile.worship: CSI liturgy and free forms in many Indian languages.

traditions.status: Active; one of the largest Protestant churches in India.

traditions.name: Church of North India
traditions.summary: Inaugurated at Nagpur in 1970 by six churches, including — unusually — Baptists, Brethren and Disciples alongside Anglicans, Methodists, Presbyterians and Congregationalists. It accepted both infant and believers' baptism and the historic episcopate. It is a member of the Anglican Communion, the World Methodist Council and the World Communion of Reformed Churches.

profile.authority: Scripture and the ecumenical creeds.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (infant or believer) and the Lord's Supper; confirmation.
profile.eschatology: Classical Christian hope.
profile.governance: Episcopal-synodical: Synod, Moderator and diocesan bishops.
profile.worship: Liturgical and free worship in Hindi and many languages.

traditions.status: Active.

traditions.name: United Church of Canada
traditions.summary: Formed in 1925 by Canadian Methodists, Congregationalists, most Presbyterians and western local union churches. Long Canada's largest Protestant church, it has been a progressive voice: it ordained Lydia Gruchy (1936), approved the ordination of gay and lesbian people (1988) and apologised for its role in the Indian residential schools. Its membership has declined sharply since the 1960s.
distinctives: Progressive positions on sexuality and justice

profile.authority: Scripture as primary source, with the Basis of Union and later statements (A Song of Faith, 2006).
profile.salvation: Grace of God in Christ for all; personal and social transformation.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Hope for God's reign of justice and peace.
profile.governance: Presbyterian-conciliar: congregations, regional councils and a General Council with a Moderator.
profile.worship: Reformed and Methodist worship traditions; Voices United hymnal.

traditions.status: Active; declining.

traditions.name: Uniting Church in Australia
traditions.summary: Formed in 1977 by Methodists, most Presbyterians and most Congregationalists on the theologically substantial Basis of Union (1971). It is the third-largest denomination in Australia and a major provider of community services (UnitingCare). It entered a covenant with its Aboriginal and Islander members (1994) and affirmed the First Peoples in its constitution's Preamble (2009). In 2018 it allowed ministers to conduct same-sex marriages.
distinctives: Basis of Union as founding theological charter
Covenant with Uniting Aboriginal and Islander Christian Congress
Ordination of women from the start

profile.authority: Scripture as unique prophetic and apostolic testimony, with the ecumenical creeds and Reformation witnesses named in the Basis of Union.
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
profile.sacraments: Baptism (infants and believers) and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: The church as a pilgrim people moving toward a promised goal.
profile.governance: Inter-conciliar: congregation, presbytery, synod and assembly.
profile.worship: Reformed and Methodist worship; Uniting in Worship.

traditions.status: Active; c. 673,000 people identified with it in the 2021 census.

traditions.name: United Church of Christ (USA)
traditions.summary: Formed in 1957 by the Evangelical and Reformed Church (German Reformed and Lutheran-Reformed 'Evangelical' roots) and the Congregational Christian Churches (New England Puritan heritage). Theologically liberal and congregational in polity, it ordained the first openly gay minister in a mainline church (William R. Johnson, 1972), and endorsed same-sex marriage (2005). Its motto: 'That they may all be one' (John 17:21).
distinctives: Union of Congregational and German Reformed/Evangelical streams
Statement of Faith (1959) as testimony, not test

profile.authority: Scripture and the historic creeds as testimonies; freedom of conscience.
profile.salvation: Grace of God in Christ for all.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and Holy Communion.
profile.eschatology: Hope for the realm of God.
profile.governance: Congregational covenant with associations, conferences and General Synod.
profile.worship: Diverse Reformed worship; New Century Hymnal.

traditions.status: Active; declining.

traditions.name: United Church of Christ in Japan (Nihon Kirisuto Kyodan)
traditions.summary: Japan's largest Protestant church, formed in 1941 when the government required Protestant denominations to unite under the Religious Organizations Law. After 1945 several groups withdrew, but the Kyodan continued as a united church of mainly Presbyterian, Methodist and Congregational heritage. Its 1967 Confession on Responsibility during the Second World War acknowledged its wartime complicity; Kyodan members in Okinawa have played a prominent role in peace activism.
distinctives: United Protestant church in a minority setting
Theological debate over the church and the emperor system

profile.authority: Scripture with the Apostles' Creed and the Kyodan Confession of Faith (1954).
profile.salvation: Salvation by grace through faith in Christ.
profile.sacraments: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.
profile.eschatology: Classical Christian hope.
profile.governance: Presbyterian-conciliar: districts and General Assembly.
profile.worship: Reformed and Methodist forms of worship.
